name: Margi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hoffmann, Carl. 1963. A Grammar of the Margi Language. London: Oxford University Press for the International African Institute. xix+287 pp.
catalog_locator: Part 'Phonology', section 'Tones', §33, p. 33 (table-of-contents fragment: 'Syllabic nasals (§ 32) 32 Tones (§ 33-34) 33 Change of tone (§ 35) 35'); text recovered as archive.org full-text-index fragments of the restricted scan grammarofmargila0000hoff
catalog_quote: TONES 33. Like many other African languages Margi is a tone language, i.e. each syllable in a Margi word or sentence has its own pitch, and this pitch is as much an essential element of that syllable as its consonant(s) and vowel(s). This does not mean that the tone(s) of a word could be [...] defined by terms of music, as it is not the absolute highness or lowness of a tone which matters [...] highness and lowness in comparison with the tones of surrounding syllables or with the average tone level of the speaker's voice. Margi has two tone levels: high and low. Besides these two level tones there is a rising tone, which must be considered a combination of a low with a high tone, although [...]. Falling tones (from high to low) are extremely rare. The tones are indicated by accents over the vowels (or syllabic nasals) ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Margi is a two-level (H/L) tone language with a derived rising (LH) tone and rare falling tones; every syllable carries a lexical/grammatical pitch. Hoffmann gives no statement about word stress or prominence at all: the only occurrences of 'stress' in the full-text index are the emphasis sense in syntax sections (e.g. 'some stress on the subject'), and stress+syllable, stress+tone, intensity, loudness, prominence return zero hits. The two open phonology articles (Maddieson 1987, Tranel 1992) are likewise silent on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: §35 'Change of tone' notes tone is not invariable and tone change has syntactic functions (e.g. interrogatives); questions may be 'spoken louder than usual' (intonation, not word stress).
new_statements.domain_note: The tone statement is about syllables in 'a Margi word or sentence'. The quote is assembled from overlapping scanned fragments returned by archive.org's full-text index (Open Library search-inside API) for the access-restricted scan; gaps between verified fragments are marked [..]. The page itself could not be viewed; it should be checked against p. 33 of the OUP 1963 or Routledge 2017/2019 edition before the entry is finalized.
new_statements.identity_note: Hoffmann 1963 describes 'Margi' proper (= Marghi Central, marg1265, the Bura-Margi group of Central Chadic); the grammar's introduction states that West Margi and South Margi are 'entirely excluded' (fragment in ol_inside/). South Margi corresponds to Glottolog Marghi South (ISO mfm, likely marg1266) and West Margi/Putai to Putai (ISO mfl, likely puta1245); both are outside this entry. Tranel 1992 and Maddieson 1987 both work from Hoffmann's data (Maddieson also from UCLA recordings of a Margi speaker), i.e. the same variety.

tone_statements.citation: Tranel, Bernard (1992/94). Tone sandhi and vowel deletion in Margi. Studies in African linguistics 23. pp. 111-183.
tone_statements.quote: [p.115] There are four surface tones in Margi (§33): two level tones (a low tone and a high tone) and two contour tones (a rising tone and a falling tone). The level tones and the rising tone are commonplace, but falling tones are "extremely rare". [p.116] As shown in Pulleyblank [1986: 195-7], the lexical entries of verb stems in Margi can be inherently toneless (Hoffmann's "changing verbs"; §210), or they can be specified with one of three unlinked tonal melodies: L ("low-tone verbs"), H ("high-tone verbs"), and LH ("rising-tone verbs").
tone_statements.locator: p. 115, section 2 'Background on Margi tones' and p. 116, section 3
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H, L; rising (common) and falling (rare) surface tones are derived LH/HL clusters on one vowel; verb stems bear melodies L, H, LH or none; floating tones central. Fn. 4: downstep 'apparently not available'. Two nouns get lexical HL (p. 178). Data: Hoffmann 1963. Nothing on stress.

sources.quote: There are four surface tones in Margi (§33): two level tones (a low tone and a high tone) and two contour tones (a rising tone and a falling tone). The level tones and the rising tone are commonplace, but falling tones are "extremely rare".
sources.locator: p. 115, Section 2 'Background on Margi tones'; data-source statement p. 114: 'All Margi data cited in this paper are taken from Hoffmann [1963]'
sources.note: Two-level-tone system (L, H) with derived contours: rising tones analysed as LH clusters on a single tone-bearing unit (Hoffmann's 'combination of a low with a high tone', §33) arising from tone trapping (lexical insufficiency or vowel deletion: Apocope, Syncope, Elision, Reduplication); falling tones (~a dozen in Hoffmann) confined to 'expressive items' (emphatic vocative suffix, sentence emphasizer, interjections, kashli + V-initial verb) and derived by Falling-Tone Formation. Verb stems lexically toneless or with unlinked L, H or LH melodies (after Pulleyblank 1986), toneless vowels get L b
